desc: MKULTRA is the documented American precedent for everything this board argues about compartmented programmes and their records. It was authorized by the Director of Central Intelligence in April 1953 as a funding mechanism whose normal procedures for project approval, funding and accounting were waived, and it ran through 149 numbered subprojects at universities, foundations, hospitals and prisons that were in most cases not told whose money it was. Its own Inspector General wrote in 1963 that the practice was to keep no records of the planning and approval of test programmes. In January 1973 the surviving files were destroyed on a verbal order. What defeated the destruction was an administrative accident: one branch's Budget and Fiscal Section had sent its finance folders to the Retired Records Center in 1970 in a departure from normal procedure that the Agency itself could not later explain, and those seven boxes were found in 1977 by an employee working a Freedom of Information Act request. The board's own MKULTRA hearing node argues from this programme without carrying it.

dossier.narrative: The argument for putting MKULTRA on a board about a legacy recovery programme is not that the two are the same subject. It is that MKULTRA is the case where every mechanism this board alleges was later proven on the government's own paper, and can therefore be used as a calibration rather than as an analogy. The Inspector General's survey of 26 July 1963 states the purpose in the Agency's own words and states, in the same document, that normal procedures for project approval, funding and accounting were waived and that present practice was to maintain no records of the planning and approval of test programs. That is a compartment designed to leave no trail, described by its own auditor. Ten years later the trail that did exist was destroyed: Technical Services Division personnel burned the files in January 1973 on Sidney Gottlieb's verbal order, itself carrying out a verbal order from DCI Helms, and both men later testified to it. The Rockefeller Commission and the Church Committee investigated the programme in 1975 without the finance file, because the 1975 searches covered the records of every branch thought likely to hold MKULTRA papers and not the Budget and Fiscal Section's retired holdings. What broke it open was administrative accident plus a statute. One branch had sent its finance folders to the Retired Records Center in 1970 in a departure from normal procedure the Agency could not later explain, and in 1977 an employee working John Marks's Freedom of Information Act request found them. The Senate's own opening statement puts the lesson plainly: one individual, through a Freedom of Information request, accomplished what two US Senate committees could not. Everything on this board about custody, about destruction orders and about what survives them has a documented instance here.

dossier.whatItIs: The CIA's umbrella project for research and development of materials to control human behavior, authorized by Director of Central Intelligence Allen W. Dulles in April 1953 and run out of the Technical Services Division through 149 numbered subprojects at universities, foundations, hospitals and prisons. Its normal procedures for project approval, funding and accounting were waived. Its records were destroyed in January 1973 on a verbal order, and seven boxes of finance folders survived only because they had been misfiled to the Retired Records Center in 1970.
dossier.whyImplicated: It is the documented American precedent for the whole of this board's argument about compartmented programmes and their records: a waived-procedure compartment, an Inspector General finding that the practice was to keep no records of the planning and approval of test programmes, a destruction order that two Senate committees could not defeat, and a single Freedom of Information Act request that did. The board's own MKULTRA hearing node argued from this programme for two months without carrying it.
